extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters learning how to write event news/features
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and feature-writing for public events (fairs, openings, parades, unveilings), using example newspaper pieces to demonstrate stylistic choices, structure, and content to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare stories with reference to style and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — The next two stories, which describe a pageant parade, should be compared with reference to style and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit pedagogical instruction: when using paired examples, evaluate differences in style and tone (e.g., laconic vs. florid, ironic vs. celebratory). Use the two parade pieces as a direct comparison exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative scene-setting and sensory detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vivid, sensory description to recreate the atmosphere for the reader (e.g., 'The effect of the place is kaleidoscopic... a perfect jumble of color and sound').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include auditory and visual images (bands playing, horns tooting, animals cackling), metaphors and similes, and panoramic details to immerse readers. Avoid dry lists when an evocative lead or scene can establish mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the most newsworthy fact/time/place/action
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the story with a clear, immediate account of the central action or moment (e.g., 'Just at midnight an electric train... slipped out of the Nineteenth street station').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front-load the key element (time, place, event) so readers know what happened at once. A strong lead orients and draws readers into details that follow; avoid subordinating the main fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific names, titles, numbers and direct quotations to establish authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Support reportage with concrete facts: attendance figures, names and titles of officials, direct letters or speeches (e.g., Roosevelt's letter, attendance estimated 'between 60,000 and 80,000 persons').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact figures, full names, offices/titles, and verbatim quotes where available. These details lend credibility and allow readers to assess significance. Where numbers are estimates, report the range and source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest anecdotes and vivid small-scale incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Enliven event coverage with short, telling anecdotes (e.g., a rooster with stage-fright, trained hens operating a turnstile, a man 'coming up smiling' from a bathtub float, a 98-year-old marcher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select concrete, humanizing moments to illustrate larger themes. Such anecdotes provide color and memorability; avoid overgeneralization without illustrative scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document organizational details, credits and program order for ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: For dedications and formal ceremonies, list committees, participating societies, speakers, program order, and contingency plans (e.g., committee membership, list of delegations, who will speak, and alternate indoor location if weather fails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record who organized the event, honorary figures, sequence of proceedings, and practical details (time/place, who unveils, letters placed in pedestal). This allows archival completeness and informs readers of institutional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory the variety and scope of exhibits and attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the range of exhibits and entertainments present — livestock, farm devices, side shows, floats, booths, special exhibits (e.g., fowl cages, duck pond, Looney Lane sideshows, suffrage booth, National Security League displays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers a sense of scale and diversity by enumerating major categories and notable singular items. Balance summary with standout specifics so the reader gets both breadth and memorable highlights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain logistical and operational aspects and notable incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on how events operated and any operational incidents that affected them (e.g., parade gaps because motorcycles couldn't stop, train hesitated at state boundary light, market reconstruction and financing details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover organization, transportation, timing, causes of notable delays or anomalies, and practical implications for attendees. This explains why the event unfolded as it did and is useful for readers and record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and characterization to portray social atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight social contrasts and character types at events to portray the crowd and culture (e.g., 'the millionaire rubbed elbows with the farm boy', 'plain people and varnished people').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ selective contrasts and portraiture to sketch social texture — clothing, behavior, interactions. This helps place events in social context and gives depth beyond mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report outcomes, awards and authoritative judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude or include results and rulings from competitive or judged elements (e.g., winners of cups and classes in horse shows, prize offerings and judges' names for decorated cars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List winners, awards, judging panels and criteria where available. For competitions, readers expect results and authoritative sources (names of judges, prize amounts).
